# YAML Metadata

  YAML are the document-level instructions on how to process and present your .qmd. 
  There are a ton of options and we will go over just a few. For a more comprehensive list 
  check out Greg Martin's [Customize with YAML](https://rpubs.com/drgregmartin/1266674)
    

```markdown
---
title: "My Personal Quarto Cheat Sheet"
author: #List of authors using hyphens
  - Jeremiah Blondeau
  - Tyler Smith
date: today #This will automatically fill in everytime you render
format: # these are the instructions on how to render to doc
  html:
    theme: yeti #there are many built in themes
    toc: true #Add a table of contents
    number-sections: true #Number each section and subsection 
    code-fold: show
bibliography: references.bib #location of bibliography
# nocite: '@*' Uncomment this to cite all references in .bib even if not directly cited in document
---
```



# Section headers

Use hash symbols for section headers. The number of hashes determines
the level.

``` markdown

## Headers
### Level 3 Header
#### Level 4 Header
##### Level 5 Header
###### Level 6 Header
```

## Headers

### Level 3 Header

#### Level 4 Header

##### Level 5 Header

###### Level 6 Header

# Tabsets

<!-- Note: Tabsets render properly in HTML output. In PDF or MS Word, they fall back to standard sequential headers. -->

``` markdown
wrap the set of headers you want as tabsets with triple ::: 
(this is called a fence)

::: panel-tabset *opening fence with panel-tabset option
## Tab 1

This is the content for the first tab.

## Tab 2

::: panel-tabset *opening fence nested

### Nested Tab 1

Content for nested tab 1

### Nested Tab 2

Content for nested tab 2

::: *closing fence nested

::: *closing fence
```

:::: panel-tabset
## Tab 1

This is the content for the first tab.

## Tab 2

::: panel-tabset
### Nested Tab 1

Content for nested tab 1

### Nested Tab 2

Content for nested tab 2
:::
::::

# Loading libraries & Reading in data

This should be done at the top of your quarto doc, typically after the
yaml, and all wrapped in a R code chunk. All the loaded data will then
be available throughout the rest of your document.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: fenced 


# Loading all your libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# Reading in data
# Example: my_data <- read_csv("path/to/data.csv")
# For this cheat sheet, we will use the built-in mtcars dataset
my_data <- mtcars
```

# Code chunks with options

```{r}
#| label: demo-options
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Common chunk options:
# echo: true/false -> Show or hide the code in the output.
# eval: true/false -> Run or do not run the code.
# warning: false   -> Suppress warnings.
# message: false   -> Suppress messages.
# include: false   -> Run the code, but hide both code and output.

print("This code is shown (echo: true) but not executed (eval: false).")

```

# Inserting figures and figure captions

```{r}
#| label: fig-mpg
#| fig-cap: "Scatterplot of Car Weight vs. MPG"
#| echo: fenced

ggplot(my_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Weight", y = "Miles Per Gallon")

```

::: callout-tip
## Tip

Notice how we labeled the figure above with the option #\| label:
fig-mpg

We can then reference that figure in our text, for example...

As shown in @fig-mpg, heavier cars typically have lower MPG.
:::

# Table outputs

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Average MPG by Cylinder Count"
#| echo: fenced

my_data |> 
  group_by(cyl) |> 
  summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg)) |> 
  kable() # kable() makes a clean markdown table

```

::: callout-tip
## Tip

This time we labeled the table above with the option #\| label:
tbl-summary

We can then reference that table in our text.

Please refer to @tbl-summary for the exact averages.
:::

# Inserting Images

``` markdown
![](images/cmes_logo.jpg){fig-align="center" width=50% .lightbox}

notice the addiional options set in the {}
fig-align="center" - centers the image
width = 50% - scaled the original photo
.lightbox - when user clicks on image full resolution pops up
```

![](images/cmes_logo.jpg){.lightbox fig-align="center" width="50%"}

# Formulas with LaTeX

``` markdown
Insert inline math equations using a single dollar sign: $y = mx + b$.

For centered display equations, use double dollar signs:

$$E = mc^2$$
```

Insert inline math equations using a single dollar sign: $y = mx + b$.

For centered display equations, use double dollar signs:

$$E = mc^2$$

## Common example equations to get a feel for LaTex syntax

1.  Fractions

``` markdown
$$
\frac{1.5}{2.3}
$$
```

$$
\frac{1.5}{2.3}
$$

2.  Super and Sub Scripts

``` markdown
$$
Y = X_1 + X_2
$$

$$
Y = X^ + X^2
$$
```

$$
Y = X_1 + X_2
$$ $$
Y = X^ + X^2
$$

3.  Square Roots

``` markdown
$$
\sqrt{p^2}
$$
```

$$
\sqrt{p^2}
$$

4.  A little bit of everything

``` markdown
$$
x_1 = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}
$$
```

$$
x_1 = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}
$$

5.  Linear Models

``` markdown
$$
Y \sim X\beta_0 + X\beta_1 + \epsilo
$$
```

$$
Y \sim X\beta_0 + X\beta_1 + \epsilon
$$

    In the above equations we used some common named symbols. Here are a
    few more...

    ``` markdown
     $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\theta$, $\pi$, $\mu$
    ```

    $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\theta$, $\pi$, $\mu$

# Citations

## Adding references to quarto document

1.  Open your .qmd file in RStudio's **Visual Editor mode**, go to the top menu, 
and click Insert > Citation.... You can search databases (like DOI, Crossref,
DataCite, or PubMed). RStudio will automatically create a references.bib 
file for you

2.  Open the YAML metadata block at the very top of your Quarto document
and add the bibliography field pointing to your .bib file

```yaml
---
title: "My Research Document"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
bibliography: references.bib
---
```

3.  Insert Citations in the Text

``` markdown
- Standard citation: This is a great paper [@heidmann2024].
- In-text citation: @ault2024 has some cool things too.
- Multiple citations: Several authors agree [@heidmann2024; @grove2024].
```

- Standard citation: This is a great paper [@heidmann2024].
- In-text citation: @ault2024 has some cool things too.
- Multiple citations: Several authors agree [@heidmann2024; @grove2024].
